statement: Classic Maya royal succession was generally patrilineal, but with documented, monumentally-inscribed female-ruler exceptions. Lady Six Sky (Ix Wak Chan Ajaw) of Naranjo reigned as de facto queen 682-693 CE, then as regent/power-behind-the-throne for her son (formally enthroned) c. 693-741 CE — contemporary scholarship treats her as the effective decision-maker even after her son's formal accession. Lady K'abel of El Perú-Waka' ruled the Wak kingdom jointly with her husband c. 672-692 CE as a representative of the Kaanul ("Snake") dynasty of Calakmul, her authority derived partly from her natal dynasty's imperial reach — a documented mechanism (marriage alliance carrying political capital) distinct from simple hereditary queenship. These are individually documented exceptions operating within a patrilineal system, not evidence of general gender parity in Classic Maya political authority.

sources.citation: Doyle, James A. On the regency of Lady Six Sky at Naranjo (Vanderbilt Undergraduate Research Journal article; academia.edu paper "'The heart and stomach of a king': A study of the regency of Lady Six Sky at Naranjo, Guatemala").

does_not_demonstrate: That Classic Maya political authority was generally open to women, as opposed to individually documented exceptions (Lady Six Sky, Lady K'abel) within an overall patrilineal succession system
